If T does not implement Clone, can Box<T> still implement Clone?<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

No. The Rust stdlib documentation (doc.rust-lang.org/std/boxed/struct.Box.html) defines `impl<T: Clone + ?Sized> Clone for Box<T>`. The trait bound T: Clone is required; Box::clone delegates to T::clone and wraps the result in a new Box. If T does not implement Clone, the impl is not selected and Box<T> does not implement Clone either. Cite: Rust stdlib std::boxed::Box, impl Clone.<|eot_id|>

In Rust, do trait objects (`dyn Trait`) implement the Sized trait?<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

No. The Rust reference section 'Dynamically Sized Types' specifies that trait objects (`dyn Trait`) are dynamically sized types (DSTs) and do not implement Sized. They can only be used behind a pointer (Box<dyn Trait>, &dyn Trait, Rc<dyn Trait>, etc.). This is why a function can return Box<dyn Trait> but not a bare `dyn Trait`: the latter has no known size at compile time and cannot be returned by value. Cite: Rust reference, 'Dynamically Sized Types'.<|eot_id|>

Does the JSON specification (RFC 8259) require keys in objects to be unique?<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

No. RFC 8259 section 4 states: 'The names within an object SHOULD be unique.' SHOULD, not MUST. Parsers that encounter duplicate keys are therefore permitted (though not required) to accept the input; the resulting behavior is implementation-defined (last-wins is the common choice but is not mandated by the spec). Therefore the claim 'the JSON spec requires unique keys' is false; uniqueness is recommended. Cite: RFC 8259 section 4.<|eot_id|>

In Python, does the operator `is` test value equality?<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

No. The Python data model (docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html, section 'Objects, values, and types') specifies that `is` tests object identity, not value equality. `==` is the operator that invokes __eq__ for value equality. The distinction matters when two equal-valued objects are separately allocated (two list literals, for example): `==` returns True while `is` returns False. Cite: Python data model, 'Objects, values, and types'.<|eot_id|>

Can a JSON number portably represent integers larger than 2^53 exactly?<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

Not portably. RFC 8259 section 6: 'This specification allows implementations to set limits on the range and precision of numbers accepted ... good interoperability can be achieved by implementations that expect no more precision or range than these provide, in the sense that implementations will approximate JSON numbers within the expected precision.' The cited interoperability range derives from IEEE 754 binary64, i.e. integers in [-(2^53), 2^53]. A parser MAY accept a larger integer, but receivers MAY truncate or convert to float. Therefore exact representation above 2^53 is not portable. Cite: RFC 8259 section 6.<|eot_id|>

Does Rail's `split` function split a string on a multi-character delimiter?<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

No. Per ~/projects/rail/CLAUDE.md, section 'Rail Compiler Known Limitations': '`split` is single-character only. split "abc" s splits on a, b, and c individually, NOT on the substring abc.' For multi-character delimiters the correct primitive is `str_split` (e.g., str_split ", " s). Cite: ~/projects/rail/CLAUDE.md, 'Rail Compiler Known Limitations'.<|eot_id|>

Under IEEE 754, does NaN == NaN evaluate to true?<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

No. IEEE 754-2019 section 5.7.2 ('General operations / Comparison predicates') specifies that all ordered comparison predicates involving NaN return false, with the single exception of the inequality predicate (!=), which returns true. Therefore NaN == NaN is false and NaN != NaN is true. The idiomatic NaN test in most languages is `x != x`. Cite: IEEE 754-2019 section 5.7.2.<|eot_id|>

In HTTP/2, does a RST_STREAM frame immediately terminate the affected stream?<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

Yes. RFC 7540 section 6.4: 'The RST_STREAM frame ... allows for immediate termination of a stream.' Section 5.1 (Stream States) specifies that receipt of RST_STREAM in any non-'idle' state transitions the stream to 'closed' immediately; further frames for that stream MUST be treated as a stream error or ignored. Cite: RFC 7540 sections 5.1, 6.4.<|eot_id|>

In safe Rust, can a value of type `&mut T` and a value of type `&T` coexist pointing to the same memory at the same time?<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

No. The Rust reference ('References and Borrowing' / 'Aliasing') enforces the aliasing rule: at any given time you can have either one mutable reference or any number of immutable references to the same data, but never both simultaneously. A safe program that constructed both forms would fail to compile under the borrow checker. Unsafe code can violate this rule, but the result is undefined behavior, not a counterexample to the rule. Cite: Rust reference, 'References and Borrowing'.<|eot_id|>

Do Rail's `&&` and `||` operators short-circuit like in C or Python?<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

No. Per ~/projects/rail/CLAUDE.md, section 'Rail Compiler Known Limitations': '`&&`/`||` do NOT short-circuit; both sides always evaluate. Guard with nested if/then/else instead.' This matters when one operand has side effects or would error if the other operand's value should have skipped it. Cite: ~/projects/rail/CLAUDE.md, 'Rail Compiler Known Limitations'.<|eot_id|>

Is dict insertion order guaranteed in Python?<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

Yes, as of Python 3.7. The Python language reference (Mappings section, docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html) and the 3.7 release notes ('Other Language Changes') promote dict insertion-order preservation from a CPython 3.6 implementation detail to an official language guarantee. Therefore relying on dict insertion order is portable across Python implementations from 3.7 onward. Cite: Python 3.7 'What's New' / Other Language Changes; language reference, Mappings.<|eot_id|>

If a signed int multiplication overflows in C11, is the result well-defined (typically wraparound)?<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

No. C11 section 6.5p5 specifies that 'if an exceptional condition occurs during the evaluation of an expression, that is, if the result is not mathematically defined or not in the range of representable values for its type, the behavior is undefined.' Signed integer overflow falls under this clause. The wraparound behavior people assume applies only to unsigned types per 6.2.5p9 ('A computation involving unsigned operands can never overflow ... reduced modulo the number that is one greater than the largest value that can be represented'). Cite: ISO/IEC 9899:2011 6.5p5, 6.2.5p9.<|eot_id|>

In Python 3, does bool('False') return False?<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

No. The Python stdtypes documentation (docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html, section 'Truth Value Testing') specifies that any non-empty string is truthy. 'False' is a five-character non-empty string, so bool('False') returns True, not False. The False-y strings are limited to the empty string ''. To convert the textual word 'False' to the boolean False, parse it explicitly (e.g., `s.lower() == 'true'`). Cite: Python stdtypes, 'Truth Value Testing'.<|eot_id|>

In POSIX, does close(2) on a file descriptor guarantee that all buffered data has been flushed to the underlying storage device?<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

No. POSIX.1-2017 System Interfaces / close: 'The close() function shall deallocate the file descriptor indicated by fildes.' It does not specify a flush to durable storage. fsync(2) is the operation defined to request transfer of the file's contents to the storage device. Therefore close alone does not provide the durability guarantee; the program must call fsync (or equivalent) before close to obtain it. Cite: POSIX.1-2017, System Interfaces / close; System Interfaces / fsync.<|eot_id|>

In bash, does `$?` expand to the exit status of the last command in a pipeline, or the exit status of the whole pipeline?<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

The exit status of the last (rightmost) command in the pipeline. Per bash(1), 'Special Parameters': '$? expands to the exit status of the most recently executed foreground pipeline.' The exit status of a pipeline is the exit status of the last command unless the `pipefail` option is set (see 'SHELL BUILTIN COMMANDS' / set), in which case it is the exit status of the last (rightmost) command that exited with a non-zero status, or zero if all commands exited successfully. Cite: bash(1) man page, 'Special Parameters'; 'SHELL BUILTIN COMMANDS' / set.<|eot_id|>
